evidence: Mart. 10.51.16: quae tua sunt, tibi habē
Varro in Gell. 15.19.2: ut tuus pistor bonum faceret pānem
terms.comment: Agrees with the thing owned. “Yours” is the same word as a predicate: quae tua sunt, what is yours. Where the owner is plain, Latin leaves the possessive out: Ostende hūc manūs, show me your hands.

evidence: Verg. A. 1.573: urbem quam statuō, vestra est
terms.comment: For more than one owner: vestra est, it is yours.

phrases.latin: quae tua sunt, tibi habē: quae mea, redde mihi
phrases.english: What is yours, keep for yourself; what is mine, give back to me.

phrases.latin: sī, quantum operae sūmpsistī ut tuus pistor bonum faceret pānem, ejus duodecimam philosophiae dedissēs, ipse bonus jam prīdem essēs factus
phrases.english: If you had given philosophy a twelfth of the trouble you took to make your baker bake good bread, you would long ago have become a good man yourself.

phrases.latin: Stultum est querī dē adversīs, ubi culpa est tua.
phrases.english: It is foolish to complain of bad luck when the fault is your own.

phrases.latin: vēnit ad nōs Cicerō tuus ad cēnam, cum Pompōnia forīs cēnāret
phrases.english: Your boy Cicero came to us for dinner, as Pomponia was dining out.

phrases.latin: Ostende hūc manūs. — Em tibi, ostendī, eccās.
phrases.english: Show me your hands. — There you are, I’ve shown them: here they are.
The city I am founding is yours.

phrases.latin: Bene ambulētis, et sit Deus in itinere vestrō, et angelus ejus comitētur vōbīscum.
phrases.english: Have a good journey; God be on your way, and his angel go with you.

sources: Lewis & Short: tuus · Lewis & Short: vester
